content: To support countries in developing national policies and programs that ensure universal access to assistive technology, the International Society of Prosthetics and Orthotics (ISPO) serves as a global, multidisciplinary, non-governmental organization. Its mission is to enhance the quality of life for individuals who benefit from prosthetic, orthotic, mobility, and assistive devices. ISPO provides a platform for the exchange of knowledge and communication on all aspects of science, practice, and education related to prosthetic and orthotic care, rehabilitation engineering, wheelchairs, therapy, and other related fields. Its activities include promoting multidisciplinary practices, facilitating professional education to improve care quality, advancing research and evidence-based practices, fostering innovative and appropriate technologies, encouraging international collaboration and consensus, and enabling knowledge exchange. The International Society of Wheelchair Professionals (ISWP), established in 2015, aims to serve as a global resource for coordinating wheelchair service standards and provision through advocacy, education, standards, evidence-based practices, and innovation. It also provides a platform for information exchange. ISWP’s outputs include tools such as the Wheelchair Basic Test, certification programs, a trainer’s certificate, the Wheelchair Educators’ Package (WEP), the Wheelchair International Network (WIN) website, a Product Wiki, and a policy advocacy toolkit. These resources aim to promote quality and appropriate wheelchair assessment and provision. The Global Partnership for Assistive Technology (ATscale) addresses the prioritization, coordination, and investment in assistive technology, as well as market challenges in key product areas at both global and national levels. ATscale is a cross-sector partnership with a mission to catalyze change, amplify existing efforts, and mobilize stakeholders with unified strategies to strengthen the enabling ecosystem. It aims to increase the availability and accessibility of affordable and appropriate assistive technology. The World Health Organization (WHO) provides evidence-based recommendations and implementation guidance to help countries and stakeholders develop or strengthen essential, affordable, accessible, effective, efficient, safe, and sustainable wheelchair services. Four service-level recommendations emphasize the critical role of wheelchair services and their personnel in ensuring an individualized approach to wheelchair selection, fitting, training, and follow-up for each user. Three system-level recommendations support seamless and coordinated wheelchair provision through well-defined referral networks, promoting equitable and effective access to wheelchairs for all in need. Continuous monitoring, evaluation, and improvement processes are recommended to enhance outcomes for individuals and overall service efficiency. WHO recommends a service model for wheelchair provision that includes individual assessment and selection, preparation and fitting of the wheelchair, user training for safe and efficient use, and follow-up to ensure the wheelchair continues to meet the user’s needs. These activities are summarized in four service steps: Select, Fit, Train, and Follow-up. These steps apply each time a person is assessed or reassessed for a new wheelchair. The service model requires accessible, barrier-free physical spaces equipped to provide a safe environment for users and personnel while ensuring privacy. The first service step, Select, involves individualized assessment and selection of wheelchairs. This process requires collaboration between the wheelchair user and appropriately trained personnel to define the user’s physical, functional, environmental, and lifestyle needs and preferences. The assessment results guide the selection of the most suitable wheelchair and its features, including cushions, postural support devices, and propulsion options. The process also identifies the user’s training needs for task-specific skills. Selection ensures that the wheelchair accommodates the user’s postural support and pressure management needs while enabling them to achieve their activity and participation goals. Many users may require more than one type of wheelchair to meet their full participation needs, such as urban and rural terrain wheelchairs or a combination of manual and power wheelchairs. To ensure wheelchair users receive devices that meet their individual needs, preferences, and goals, a sufficient variety of products must be available. No single model or size of wheelchair can meet the needs of all users, and a limited range of options can result in inappropriate devices for most users. Member States should ensure the availability of a range of manual and, where possible, power wheelchairs, cushions, postural supports, and other accessories to address the diversity of user needs. This selection should enable the majority of users to achieve optimal mobility, seating, postural support, and participation in various activities and environments. WHO and UNICEF have collaborated to increase the availability of affordable, quality assistive products through initiatives such as developing assistive product specifications for 26 priority products, including wheelchairs, and publishing a procurement manual. These resources assist countries in procurement processes and signal manufacturers and suppliers regarding minimum requirements for assistive products. New assistive products have been introduced to UNICEF and WHO supply catalogs to increase global availability and affordability. These catalogs include various types of wheelchairs, cushions, and accessories to support diverse needs across child and adult users in different settings and levels of complexity. Wheelchair features that impact outcomes include frame design (folding or rigid), overall weight, seat angle and height, foot and armrest designs, rear wheel position adjustability, and front caster width and diameter. For power wheelchairs, features such as drive wheel position, power seat functions, and programming adjustability are critical. Postural support is influenced by adjustable seat-to-backrest angles, seat depth, and the potential to add off-the-shelf or locally fabricated supports. Participation in different environments, such as urban or rough terrain, depends on frame design, weight, wheelbase, and durability. Member States can ensure a minimum, well-selected range of customizable or adjustable wheelchairs by establishing a nationally agreed priority list of assistive technology, including wheelchairs, cushions, and postural supports.
